content.text: Stars are born, live, and die over billions of years. Understanding stellar evolution helps us comprehend where the elements came from—including those that make up our bodies. The life cycle of a star depends primarily on its initial mass, determining whether it ends as a white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole.

A star's life cycle is determined by its initial mass. Low-mass stars (like our Sun) end as white dwarfs, while high-mass stars end in spectacular supernovae, leaving behind neutron stars or black holes.

items.title: Nebula
items.description: A vast cloud of gas (mainly hydrogen) and dust. Gravity causes regions to collapse and compress, beginning the process of star formation.

items.title: Protostar
items.description: A dense, hot core forms as material collapses under gravity. Not yet fusing hydrogen. Continues to contract and heat over millions of years.

items.title: Main Sequence Star
items.description: Core reaches ~15 million degrees C and hydrogen fusion begins. Radiation pressure balances gravity, creating a stable star. This phase lasts billions of years for Sun-like stars.

items.title: Red Giant / Red Supergiant
items.description: Core hydrogen is depleted. The core contracts and heats while outer layers expand and cool. Low-mass stars become red giants; high-mass stars become red supergiants that fuse heavier elements up to iron.

items.title: Planetary Nebula / Supernova
items.description: Low-mass stars gently eject outer layers as a planetary nebula. High-mass stars undergo a catastrophic supernova explosion, creating elements heavier than iron and scattering them into space.

items.title: Stellar Remnant
items.description: Low-mass stars leave behind a white dwarf that slowly cools. High-mass stars leave a neutron star (1.4-3 solar masses) or black hole (>3 solar masses).

Describe the stages in the life of a star like our Sun.
Hydrogen fusion begins, stable for ~10 billion years
Core hydrogen exhausted, outer layers expand
Explain why massive stars have shorter lifetimes than smaller stars.
Although massive stars have more hydrogen fuel:
Higher mass means higher core temperature
Higher temperature means faster fusion rate
Fuel is consumed much more quickly
A star 10× the Sun's mass might live only 10 million years (compared to Sun's 10 billion years)
Describe what happens during a supernova.
Iron accumulates in the core of a massive star
Iron fusion absorbs energy rather than releasing it
Core can no longer support itself against gravity
Core collapses in less than a second
Outer layers fall inward then rebound explosively
Star becomes briefly brighter than an entire galaxy
Heavy elements are created and scattered into space
Core remains as neutron star or black hole

content.text: — All stars eventually run out of fuel and die.
"The Sun will explode as a supernova"
— The Sun isn't massive enough. It will become a red giant then white dwarf.
— At a distance, a black hole's gravity is the same as the star it came from. It's only at close range that escape becomes impossible.
— The opposite is true. They burn fuel much faster.
"Elements were all created in the Big Bang"
— Only hydrogen, helium, and tiny amounts of lithium. Everything else comes from stars.

Students often think bigger stars live longer because they have more fuel. In fact, massive stars burn through their fuel much faster due to higher core temperatures, so they have much shorter lifetimes.
Stars form from nebulae through gravitational collapse
Main sequence: hydrogen fusion, balanced forces, stable
Low mass stars: main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
High mass stars: main sequence → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star/black hole
Fusion creates elements up to iron
Supernovae create elements heavier than iron
All heavy elements in our bodies came from ancient stars

Nebula → Protostar → Main Sequence (burns hydrogen very rapidly, lasting only a few million years) → Red Supergiant (fuses heavier elements up to iron in layered shells) → Supernova (core collapses when iron accumulates) → Black Hole (since 20 solar masses is well above the threshold, the remnant core likely exceeds 3 solar masses).
